source_text: Uerumtamen cum carnalibus animis fortasse non sic agendum est, sed descendendum est potius ad eorum cogitationes, qui naturam incorpoream et spiritalem cogitando persequi uel non audent uel nondum ualent, ita ut nec ipsam cogitationem suam eadem cogitatione considerent et inueniant eam nullo locorum spatio de ipsis locorum spatiis iudicantem. descendamus ergo ad eorum sensus et quaeramus ab eis, iuxta quam partem aut iuxta quod latus. sicut Manichaeus dicit. inlustris illius ac sanctae terrae erat tenebrarum terra. dicit enim: iuxta unam partem ac latus, nec dicit, quam partem uel quod latus. dextrum an sinistrum. sed quodlibet eligant, illud certe manifestum est non dici unum latus. nisi ubi est alterum latus. ubi autem uel tria uel plura sunt latera, aut figurae ambitus intellegitur undique terminatus aut, si ex aliqua parte in inmensum patet, ex iis tamen. quae latera dicuntur, necesse est finiatur. dicant ergo, ex alio latere uel ex aliis lateribus quid adiungebatur terrae lucis, si ex uno latere erat gens tenebrarum V non dicunt; sed cum premuntur, ut dicant, infinita esse dicunt alia latera terrae illius, quam lucis uocant. id est per infinita spatia distendi et nullo fine cohiberi. nec intellegunt iam non esse latera, quod quibusuis tardis ingeniis apertissimum est; tunc enim essent latera. si finibus suis terminarentur. quid ad me, inquit, si non sunt latera? sed cum diceres "iuxta unam partem ac latus," aliam quoque partem siue partes et aliud latus siue latera cogebas intellegi. nam si unum tantum latus erat, tantum iuxta latus dici debuit, non "iuxta unum latus." sicut in nostro corpore recte dicimus esse aliquid iuxta unum oculum, quia est alter oculus, aut iuxta unam mamillam, quia est altera. si autem dicamus iuxta unum nasum aut iuxta unum umbilicum, cum alius non sit, et a doctis et ab indoctis ridebimur. sed non te uerbis premo; fortassis enim unum quasi unicum appellare uoluisti.
orientation: Augustine is addressing Mani's claim that the land of darkness lay beside one side of the land of light, and he is now descending to the level of carnal-minded readers to show that the phrase 'one side' is self-contradictory.
pass_a_gloss: But perhaps one must not deal thus with carnal minds, but one must rather descend to the thoughts of those who either do not dare or are not yet able to pursue an incorporeal and spiritual nature by thinking, so that they do not even consider their own thought by that same thought and find that it judges about the spaces of places from no space of places. Let us therefore descend to their senses and ask them, beside which part or beside which side, as Mani says, was the land of darkness of that illustrious and holy land. For he says: beside one part and side, and he does not say which part or which side, right or left. But let them choose whatever they like, this at least is clear, that one side is not said unless where there is another side. But where there are either three or more sides, either a boundary of a figure is understood, bounded on every side, or, if it lies open to an immense extent from some part, yet from those things which are called sides it must be bounded. Let them therefore say, from another side or from other sides what was joined to the land of light, if from one side was the nation of darkness. They do not say; but when they are pressed to say, they say that the other sides of that land, which they call the land of light, are infinite, that is, that it is stretched out through infinite spaces and is bounded by no end. And they do not understand that there are no longer sides, which is most clear to any however slow minds; for then they would be sides, if they were bounded by their own ends. What does it matter to me, he says, if there are no sides? But when you were saying 'beside one part and side,' you were forcing another part or parts and another side or sides to be understood. For if there was only one side, it ought to have been said only 'beside the side,' not 'beside one side.' Just as in our body we rightly say that something is beside one eye, because there is another eye, or beside one breast, because there is another. But if we say beside one nose or beside one navel, since there is not another, we will be laughed at by both the learned and the unlearned. But I do not press you with words; for perhaps you wanted to call one as if unique.

choices.why: Augustine contrasts carnal minds with those able to consider incorporeal nature; 'minds' fits the psychological context better than 'souls' here.
The impersonal passive preserves Augustine's rhetorical move of lowering the argument to a simpler level.
The glossary requires 'land of light' for terra lucis, but here the adjective 'illustrious' is used instead; 'land' is kept literal.
Mani's myth personifies the land of darkness as a nation; 'nation' preserves the collective sense.
Augustine distinguishes 'one' as a numeral from 'unique' as 'only'; the rendering keeps the distinction explicit.

pass_b_english: But perhaps one should not deal with carnal minds in this way. Instead, one must descend to the thoughts of those who either do not dare or are not yet able to pursue an incorporeal and spiritual nature by thinking, so that they do not even consider their own thought by that same thought and find that it judges about spatial distances without itself occupying any space. So let us descend to their level of sense and ask them: next to which part, or next to which side, as Mani says, was the land of darkness located in relation to that illustrious and holy land? For he says, "next to one part and side," but he does not say which part or which side—right or left. But whichever they choose, one thing is certainly clear: you cannot speak of one side unless there is another side. And where there are three or more sides, either you mean a boundary of a shape that is enclosed on every side, or, if it opens out into immensity on some side, it must still be bounded on the sides that are called sides. So let them say what was joined to the land of light on the other side or sides, if the nation of darkness was on one side. They do not say. But when they are pressed to say, they say that the other sides of that land they call the land of light are infinite—that is, that it stretches out through infinite spaces and is held in by no limit. And they do not understand that then there are no longer sides, which is perfectly obvious even to the slowest minds. For there would be sides only if they were bounded by their own limits. "What does it matter to me," he says, "if there are no sides?" But when you said "next to one part and side," you forced us to understand another part or parts and another side or sides. For if there was only one side, you should have said only "next to the side," not "next to one side." Just as in our body we correctly say that something is next to one eye, because there is another eye, or next to one breast, because there is another. But if we say next to one nose or next to one navel, when there is no other, both the learned and the unlearned will laugh at us. But I am not pressing you on words; perhaps you wanted to call one as if unique.

last_rejected.quote: "What does it matter to me," he says, "if there are no sides?"
last_rejected.source_quote: quid ad me, inquit, si non sunt latera?
last_rejected.why: The Latin 'inquit' here introduces the imagined Manichaean interlocutor, not Mani himself, but the English 'he says' makes it ambiguous and could be read as Mani quoted.
last_rejected.fix: "What does it matter to me," your defender says, "if there are no sides?"
last_rejected.ruling: 'he says' is a standard rendering of 'inquit'; ambiguity of speaker reference is not a major meaning change.

last_rejected.why: 'gens' means 'people' or 'race,' not 'nation' in the political sense; Mani's myth refers to the race/people of darkness, not a nation-state.
last_rejected.ruling: 'gens' includes 'nation' in its normal semantic range; not a major error, just a preference for 'people' or 'race'.
